newsitem.title: FRANCE: French sailor shatters round-the-world record.
newsitem.headline: French sailor shatters round-the-world record.

text.p: French sailor Olivier de Kersauson set a new round-the-world sailing record on Monday, shaving nearly three days off the old record by circling the globe in 71 days, 14 hours, 18 minutes and eight seconds.
The previous record of 74 days 22 hours and 17 minutes had been set by New Zealander Sir Peter Blake in 1994.

De Kersauson and his crew of six, aboard his Sport-Elec trimaran yacht, crossed the finish line at 6.59 a.m. GMT, assuring him the Jules Verne trophy offered for sailing around the world in under 80 days.

"We won it, and I think that the seven of us on board here -- we went to look for it where no one else had gone, and we are truly happy," de Kersauson said as he headed to the western French port of Brest after crossing the finish line.
"There were three years of preparation, of hard and never-ending work, of risk and disappointment. But there was also the tremendous joy of racing," he told French television LCI.

Named after author Jules Verne's 1872 novel Around the World in 80 Days, the race ends at an imaginary line across the English Channel between the southernmost tip of Britain's Lizard Point and France's Ouessant Island.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe, in the midst of a closely contested parliamentary election campaign, quickly issued a congratulatory message to de Kersauson expressing his admiration.
"We are all proud of what you have accomplished," Juppe said.

President Jacques Chirac, in a separate message, said the "extraordinary victory...confirms the very great talent of our sailors and brings to France a pride and elan that can only be achieved in the winning of a great challenge."
The conservative Chirac has urged a "new elan" and a "shared elan" for France in his campaign messages urging a victory for the governing centre-right.
Tens of thousands of fans were waiting to greet de Kersauson and his crew in Brest, which they left on March 4.
Blake, on his trimaran Enza-New Zealand, had in 1994 broken a record of 79 days six hours and 15 minutes set a year earlier by France's Bruno Peyron on his trimaran Commodore explorer.
